title: Complement System in Clinical Practice
subject: Microbiology & immunology
summary: The complement system links innate immunity to inflammation, opsonisation and cell lysis. Understanding its pathways helps diagnose and manage infections and immune‑mediated disease, especially where laboratory resources are limited.

sections.p: A group of plasma proteins that, when activated, amplify inflammation, tag microbes for phagocytosis and form the membrane‑attack complex (MAC) to lyse cells.
b: Three activation routes: classical (immune complexes), lectin (MBL binding), alternative (spontaneous tick‑over).
Key effectors: C3a/C5a (anaphylatoxins), C3b (opsonin), C5b‑9 (MAC).

sections.p: Complement disorders are staged by clinical impact rather than lab values: mild (recurrent mild infections), moderate (invasive bacterial disease), severe (life‑threatening meningococcal sepsis).
b: Stage I – occasional upper‑respiratory infections.
Stage II – invasive infections (meningitis, sepsis) requiring hospitalisation.
Stage III – fulminant meningococcal disease or rapid deterioration.

sections.p: Both inherited deficiencies and acquired consumption can impair complement function.
b: Inherited C5‑C9 deficiency – classic cause of recurrent meningococcal infection in young adults.
Properdin deficiency – X‑linked, high risk of lethal meningococcal disease.
Acquired consumption: severe bacterial sepsis, systemic lupus erythematosus, HIV, malaria, schistosomiasis.
Medications: eculizumab (C5 inhibitor) – predisposes to meningococcal infection.

sections.p: Patients with complement deficiency often present with unusual or recurrent infections, especially with encapsulated organisms.
b: Recurrent Neisseria meningitidis meningitis or sepsis.
Unexplained severe cellulitis or osteomyelitis with Gram‑negative rods.
Autoimmune haemolysis when auto‑antibodies activate complement on red cells.

sections.p: Testing focuses on functional activity and individual component levels, adapted to low‑resource settings.

t.b: Is overall classical pathway activity normal? Low CH50 suggests deficiency of any C1‑C9 component; if unavailable, use a simple hemolysis test with sensitised sheep red cells.
Is the alternative pathway functional? Low AH50 points to properdin or factor B/D deficiency.
Which protein is low? Guides genetic counselling and vaccine strategy.

t.a: Blood smear for haemolysis + direct Coombs test
t.b: Is complement‑mediated haemolysis occurring? Positive Coombs with C3d indicates immune‑complex activation.
Which organism is causing infection? Identifies encapsulated bacteria that exploit complement gaps.

sections.p: Rapid progression to septic shock in meningococcal disease is the main emergency.
b: Sudden fever, petechial rash, hypotension – treat as meningococcal sepsis.
Acute renal failure from complement‑mediated glomerulonephritis.
Severe haemolytic anaemia with jaundice.

sections.p: Treat the underlying infection, replace missing complement when possible, and prevent future episodes.
b: Empiric broad‑spectrum antibiotics covering Neisseria (e.g., ceftriaxone) while awaiting cultures.
Vaccinate against meningococcus (A, C, W, Y, B), pneumococcus and Haemophilus influenzae type b.
For inherited C5‑C9 deficiency, consider plasma‑derived complement replacement in severe infections (if available).
If on eculizumab, give meningococcal vaccine 2 weeks prior and provide prophylactic penicillin.

sections.p: Long‑term care focuses on infection prophylaxis and monitoring for autoimmune complications.
b: Annual meningococcal booster; repeat pneumococcal vaccine every 5 years.
Educate patients to seek care promptly for fever or rash.
Screen for lupus or other autoimmune disease if complement consumption is suspected.

sections.p: Conditions that mimic complement deficiency clinically.
b: Asplenia – also predisposes to encapsulated bacterial infection but has normal complement tests.
IgG subclass deficiency – leads to recurrent infections but without low CH50.
Severe neutropenia – infection risk without complement abnormalities.
Acute phase reaction can raise C3/C4, masking a partial deficiency.
Recent plasma transfusion temporarily normalises CH50, hiding an underlying defect.
Hemolysis can consume C3, giving a falsely low level unrelated to genetic deficiency.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly spreading petechial rash with fever and hypotension (meningococcal sepsis).
Acute kidney injury with haematuria in a known complement disorder.
Severe anaemia with jaundice and dark urine suggesting complement‑mediated haemolysis.

faq.q: Why do complement deficiencies predispose specifically to meningococcal infection?
faq.a: Neisseria relies on the MAC to be killed; lack of terminal components (C5‑C9) prevents lysis, allowing invasive disease.

faq.q: Can a normal CH50 rule out all complement problems?
faq.a: No; isolated lectin‑pathway defects or low C3 with normal CH50 can still cause disease.

faq.q: What prophylaxis is needed for a patient on eculizumab?
faq.a: Meningococcal vaccination plus lifelong penicillin prophylaxis because the drug blocks MAC formation.

exam: A 22‑year‑old with two episodes of meningococcal meningitis in 3 years – what investigations would you order and why? — CH50, AH50 and component ELISAs to identify a terminal‑pathway deficiency; cultures guide acute therapy.

A child with SLE presents with low C3 and C4 – how does this differ from an inherited complement deficiency? — Low C3/C4 reflects consumption; CH50 may be low but component levels are not absent, indicating disease activity rather than genetic loss.

A patient on eculizumab develops fever and a petechial rash – what is your immediate management? — Treat as meningococcal sepsis: give ceftriaxone, supportive care, and notify for possible plasma exchange; do not wait for cultures.

Explain why a patient with properdin deficiency is at higher risk of lethal meningococcal disease than a patient with C3 deficiency. — Properdin stabilises the alternative pathway, and its absence leads to complete loss of alternative‑pathway activity, removing a key early defence against Neisseria.

How would you modify your diagnostic approach if CH50 testing is unavailable? — Perform a simple hemolysis assay with sensitised sheep red cells; if absent, proceed to specific component ELISAs when possible.

What vaccination schedule would you recommend for a teenager with confirmed C5‑C8 deficiency? — Give quadrivalent meningococcal conjugate vaccine, MenB vaccine, pneumococcal conjugate vaccine, and Hib vaccine; boosters every 5 years for meningococcus.

A patient with recurrent cellulitis has normal CH50 but low AH50 – what is the most likely defect and its clinical relevance? — Properdin or factor D deficiency; predisposes to infections by encapsulated organisms, especially Neisseria.
Why is complement testing less useful during acute severe sepsis? — Massive consumption can transiently depress all components, giving a false impression of deficiency; repeat testing after recovery.
